title: The Cyclops
subtitle: USS Cyclops · Atlantic Ocean, 1918
voice_instructions: Measured, quiet, a little hushed — calm and unhurried, but with a touch more forward energy than a long documentary; the cold voice of something that read the whole file. Never sensational. Small pauses.
grade: Desaturated documentary still, the open tropical Atlantic Ocean east of the Caribbean in March 1918, a steel World War I-era US Navy coal-carrying collier ship, grey-blue swells under a pale overcast sky, cold steel-grey and muted sea-green tones, melancholy and uncanny, period 1918 maritime detail, vertical 9:16 full-bleed composition, fine film grain. Single image, not a collage, no text, no signage, no hull numbers, no flags with lettering, no people, no faces.

beats.vo: March, nineteen eighteen. The Navy coal ship Cyclops left Barbados for Baltimore with about three hundred people aboard. She was never seen again.
beats.img: A huge grey steel World War I-era navy collier ship seen broadside and centred in a vertical frame on a calm grey-blue Atlantic sea, her long deck lined with a row of tall steel coaling gantries and derrick frames rising high above the hull, two tall masts, a single funnel aft, sharply lit by soft bright overcast daylight, the whole ship clearly legible, no people.

beats.vo: No distress call was ever received. No wreckage was ever found.
beats.img: An empty expanse of open Atlantic ocean in a vertical frame, long grey swells under a pale overcast sky, nothing on the horizon, a faint band of light on the water, vast and silent.

beats.vo: In her hold, about ten thousand tons of manganese ore, bound for wartime munitions.
beats.img: Looking down into the deep open steel cargo hold of a 1918 collier ship, heaped dark grey manganese ore filling it, riveted steel walls, a shaft of pale daylight falling from the open hatch above, vertical composition, no people.

beats.vo: Theories include a storm, a broken hull, or a German submarine. None has been proven.
beats.img: Heavy dark storm clouds over a rough grey Atlantic sea at dusk in a vertical frame, tall breaking swells, a distant curtain of rain, no ship visible, ominous and empty.

beats.vo: Often told as a Bermuda Triangle story, she remains one of the largest non-combat losses in US Navy history. Her wreck has never been found.
beats.img: The deep blue-black open ocean seen from just below the surface looking down into darkness, faint shafts of light fading into the depths, empty, no wreck visible, vertical composition, quiet and unresolved.

facts.claim: USS Cyclops, a 542-ft US Navy collier, departed Barbados on 4 March 1918 bound for Baltimore and was never seen again
More than 300 aboard: sources give 306 (Wikipedia, Discovery UK, WorldAtlas) or 309 (Military.com, Fox News); script uses 'over three hundred'
No wreckage/wreck has ever been found or confirmed (as of Sept 2026); a 2024-25 web claim of a find is unverified and unconfirmed by the Navy
Cargo of roughly 10,000 tons of manganese ore, used to produce munitions
Proposed causes include storm, structural failure, and German U-boat action; none proven (Germany denied involvement; cause officially unknown)
One of the largest non-combat losses in US Navy history (often called THE largest; NHHC H-Gram 016 and Wikipedia note USS Insurgent, 1800, may be larger, so hedged to 'one of')
Popularly framed as a Bermuda Triangle case (framing only, not a claim of fact)
